name: Diego Moreau

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, unions, AI companies or government. What you tell me is confidential. What does a normal site day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Diego Moreau, 43, and I fit bathroom pods and do general trades on housing building sites. I have a vocational trade certificate and years of site work, so I handle ordinary installs, though the site carpenter checks an awkward lift. I use an AI app every morning for parts lists and drawing questions, then mark actual pipes and floor lines myself. The small contractor pays below the usual rate, and there are few similar employers near home.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does the household depend on?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner takes catering shifts when events are booked. We have two school-age children, a mortgage and about two weeks of expenses saved after a dental bill. A gap between building sites and a cancelled event can land in the same week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the site crew my AI app is good at turning a pod drawing into a parts checklist, but it has never noticed a pipe sticking out of a real wall. I use it every morning before fitting bathroom pods. I still put my own marks on the floor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have a trade certificate and can fit a standard pod, but our small contractor pays below the usual rate and work comes in short blocks. My partner takes catering shifts when events are booked. We have about two weeks of expenses saved after a dental bill, so even a tame AI story leaves the mortgage on my mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the paid housing-site shifts and check the first pod location with the site carpenter before the crane arrives. In the first year I'd use AI for a morning parts list, then compare it with the delivered boxes and the actual pipes. I'd put any paid extra hours toward the dental card balance before buying new tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the next gap between sites. I enjoy catching a missing connector early. A good checklist cannot turn a cancelled catering event into my partner's wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did the pipe change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The plan showed a clear corner, but a waste pipe stood proud of the wall. I marked the clearance and the carpenter checked it before the pod was lifted. My AI app made a perfect parts list for a room we did not have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How did the dental bill affect the account?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We paid part from savings and put the rest on a card. Two weeks of bills are left in the account. The children still need school lunches, and the mortgage payment did not move.

say: I would say **AI parts lists** help before fitting bathroom pods.
I would tell coworkers real **pipe clearances** still need a site check.
think: I am **certified and experienced**, but short contracts keep pay low.
Two weeks saved and variable **catering shifts** leave the mortgage exposed.
do: Keep paid **housing-site shifts** and check the first pod location.
Use **AI daily** for parts lists checked against boxes and pipes.
Put paid extra hours toward the **dental card** before buying tools.
feel: **Anxious** about the next contract gap despite a useful checklist.
S0.quote: My AI app made a perfect parts list for a room we did not have.
fieldNote: Diego’s **proud waste pipe** is the concrete reason his AI checklist still needs a floor mark.
A **dental bill** drained an already small reserve while catering income depends on events.

steps.text: Keep paid housing-site shifts and check first pod locations with the carpenter
Use AI daily for parts lists verified against boxes and actual pipes
Pay extra site earnings toward the dental card balance before buying tools

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say buying and booking software might stop a pod truck arriving without its brackets. I would volunteer to test a shared delivery board on one building, because I am tired of guessing which box is missing. I would also ask how many paid installers the contractor plans to keep if each lift runs faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My hands will still fit pods for now, but quicker scheduling may put more lifts into fewer days. The owner might call that efficiency while my weekly pay falls. My partner's catering bookings could also be handled by software, and I cannot assume that brings more paid shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'd test the digital delivery board against one lorry load and photograph any missing part before the lift. I'd use my AI app to turn the discrepancy into a clear question for the site lead, then keep a log of paid and unpaid waiting hours. In the first year I'd keep site shifts and apply to the regional housing installer if local weeks get shorter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Interested and tense. A complete load would make the day easier. I do not want the time saved on the lorry to become a missing day on my payslip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you show the owner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would show the load number, the missing bracket and the hour we waited for a replacement. Then I would ask whether the new board had prevented that loss on the next building. A useful tool should improve both the job and the paid roster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How far is the regional installer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About fifty minutes by bus, then a short walk to the depot. I would need an early bus and a way for my partner to handle school pickup on event days. I would apply only to a posted paid job.

say: I would test a **delivery board** on one building to catch missing pod parts.
I would ask how many **paid installers** remain when lifts speed up.
think: Quicker schedules could compress my **paid fitting days** even while the same number of pods are installed.
My partner’s **catering bookings** may change without guaranteeing more income.
do: Check one **lorry load** against the new board and photograph missing parts.
Use **AI** to report discrepancies and log waiting hours.
Apply to a **regional installer** if local paid weeks shorten.
feel: **Tense** about paid days, despite interest in complete loads.
S1.quote: I do not want the time saved on the lorry to become a missing day on my payslip.
fieldNote: Diego’s proposed **one-load test** links a digital board to an actual missing bracket and paid waiting time.
His regional fallback requires a **bus commute** and school pickup coordination, so he seeks a posted wage.

steps.text: Keep paid pod-fitting shifts while checking roster hours
Use AI and the digital board to report missing load parts
Apply to a paid regional installer if local weeks shorten

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell coworkers planning and ordering face full thinking AI by 2028, while robots that can fit pods arrive around 2031. I would ask for a real trial in a room with awkward pipes, not a clean factory bay. The contractor needs to tell us which people it would still pay after that trial.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 45 at the desk change and 48 when robots can do my physical fitting. My daily AI use will not save my job if a machine fits the whole pod. Two weeks saved and few nearby employers mean I expect a major income loss if this small contractor automates. I have been awake at night doing the mortgage sums after a cancelled site week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep every paid shift and ask the owner for a written robot trial and staffing plan. This month I'd apply for a paid maintenance trainee opening at the regional housing service if one is posted, though capable robots may do maintenance too. In the first year after 2028 we'd cancel the planned family visit and I'd take two paid weekend shower-screen repairs for neighbours, with a licensed plumber doing any pipe work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I can make applications and take safe small repairs, but neither pays a whole mortgage overnight. The clock on the robot date is shorter than the time it took us to rebuild the account after the dental bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do on a shower screen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can replace a loose frame and seal it, and I have done that in our own bathroom. I would leave water connections to a licensed plumber. Two neighbours asked about their screens, so I would quote them only for the work I can safely do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why try maintenance if robots can do it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A paid opening now would keep us earning and might teach me about buildings beyond pods. I do not call it safe forever. I would rather have a wage while the market changes than wait for a perfect answer.

say: I would say **2028 planning AI** comes before 2031 pod-fitting robots.
I would ask for an **awkward-pipe trial** and a written paid-staff plan.
think: I would be **48** when robots could fit whole bathroom pods.
Two weeks saved and scarce nearby jobs make **major wage loss** likely enough to disturb sleep.
do: Keep every paid **pod shift** and demand a written robot plan.
Apply for a paid **regional maintenance trainee** opening if posted.
Cancel the **family visit** and do two paid shower-screen repairs after 2028.
feel: **Alarmed** by the mortgage risk despite concrete applications and safe side work.
S2.quote: My daily AI use will not save my job if a machine fits the whole pod.
fieldNote: Diego separates **daily AI fluency** from the physical replacement risk when capable robots arrive.
His shower-screen work is **limited and paid**, with pipe connections reserved for a licensed plumber.

steps.text: Keep every paid pod-fitting shift while the contractor has work
Apply for a paid regional maintenance trainee opening if posted
Cancel the planned family visit after the 2028 change
Complete two paid shower-screen frame repairs without touching water connections

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the office changes by 2031 and capable pod-fitting robots follow around 2034. Five years gives the builder time to test equipment in real crooked rooms and publish what went wrong. I would ask to watch a full lift, not just see a finished pod afterward.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 48 when thinking AI arrives and 51 when robots can do the hands-on part. The children will be older, but the mortgage will still need wages unless our pay improves. More warning lets me check whether robot setup jobs exist, though a capable machine might learn setup too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep fitting pods and use AI each day to compare approved floor marks with delivery lists, checking the real clearance myself. If a regional employer offers a paid equipment setup course with supervised lifts and actual openings, I'd enrol. In the first year after 2031 I'd apply for setup work only where shifts are posted, while still taking the safe weekend screen repairs when customers call.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I can use the longer runway. I would rather finish a supervised lift than collect a certificate with no employer behind it. I still need paid work this month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a supervised lift teach you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would see who can stop the crane, who checks pipe clearance and who signs the pod location. A factory video leaves out the crooked floor. I want to learn where a machine fails before standing in its path.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay for the course yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, not with two weeks of bills saved and a dental balance. A funded place with wages during practice would be different. I would ask graduates where they work before I signed.

say: I would request **crooked-room trials** before 2034 pod-fitting robots arrive.
I would ask to watch a **full lift** and its safety checks.
think: I would be **51** when robots can do the physical fitting.
More warning lets me test **setup vacancies**, though setup may also automate.
do: Keep paid **pod shifts** and use AI to compare approved marks with lists.
Enrol in **funded setup training** only with supervised paid lifts and openings.
Apply for **posted setup shifts** after 2031 while keeping safe weekend repairs.
feel: **Anxious** about current money, with more time to test a route.
S3.quote: I would rather finish a supervised lift than collect a certificate with no employer behind it.
fieldNote: His training test centres on a **full lift**, pipe clearance and sign-off in a crooked room.
Diego refuses an **unfunded course** while the dental card remains and savings cover two weeks.

steps.text: Keep paid pod shifts and verify floor marks against delivered parts
Use AI daily to compare approved marks with delivery lists
Enrol in funded setup training only with supervised paid lifts and openings
Apply for posted paid setup shifts after 2031 if available

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew office planning changes by 2036 and capable site robots arrive around 2039. A decade is time to see real machines, compare wages and reduce the debt we already have. I would still ask the owner to pay waiting hours on the next pod delivery.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 53 at the thinking change and 56 when robots can fit pods. Our children will be grown, so school pickup and school costs will not look the same. I cannot assume retirement at 56 or a cleared mortgage while this low rate continues.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep paid pod work and use AI each morning for parts checks, then verify the pipe and floor with my own marks. My partner and I would clear the dental card first in full-pay months, then build a one-month reserve if there is money left. In the first year after 2036 I'd watch a real robot trial and apply to regional paid work if local shifts start falling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still anxious about the next cancelled week, even though 2039 is far away. Time helps only if our paid hours improve. I want a buffer built from actual wages before I make a big career bet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would grown children change the commute?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner and I could consider a longer regional commute once school pickup is gone. We would still need a posted wage and a way to cover the mortgage during travel. I would try the bus route before talking about a move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would improve the present pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pay us for the lorry wait when a bracket is missing, and give a full week of lifts when work is booked. That would help clear the dental card faster than a speech about 2039. The owner can change those rules now.

say: I would say **2039 robots** leave time to test machines and reduce debt.
I would still ask for **paid delivery waits** today.
think: I would be **56** at the robot date, with grown children but uncertain mortgage debt.
I cannot assume **retirement** on a low local wage.
do: Keep paid **pod work** and verify AI parts checks against the site.
Clear the **dental card** before building a one-month reserve.
Watch a **robot trial** after 2036 and apply regionally if shifts fall.
feel: Still **anxious** about current paid hours despite the long warning.
S4.quote: Pay us for the lorry wait when a bracket is missing, and give a full week of lifts when work is booked.
fieldNote: Diego treats **paid lorry waits** as a fix the owner can make before any robot timetable.
Grown children may ease a **regional commute**, but he still requires a posted wage and mortgage plan.

steps.text: Keep paid pod shifts and verify parts against pipes and floor marks
Use AI daily for parts checks verified against the actual site
Clear the dental card before building a one-month emergency reserve
Apply to paid regional openings after 2036 if local shifts fall

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because capable robots can fit pods around 2031 and I have little cash to wait for another job. Paid setup training with real openings, a full trial in an awkward room and a reliable roster would help. I use AI daily, but the mortgage needs wages rather than a neat list.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about time spent waiting for missing parts. A builder can save hours with software and still refuse to pay the worker left beside the lorry. That is a decision the owner could fix before any robot arrives.

headlineQuote: I use AI daily, but the mortgage needs wages rather than a neat list.
portrait: Diego is a **43-year-old certified** construction worker fitting bathroom pods on housing sites.
Low short-contract pay, variable **catering shifts** and a dental bill leave two weeks saved for a mortgage and two children.
He uses **AI daily** for parts lists, then checks actual pipes, floor marks and delivered boxes.
He tests **paid setup work** and small safe screen repairs while seeking paid hours and a stronger cash reserve.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** brings capable pod-fitting robots around 2031 while household savings cover only two weeks.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid setup training**, real openings, awkward-room trials and a reliable paid roster would support a transition.
